title: Blessings, Curses, and a Warning
overview: Moses sets out the rewards Israel can expect for staying loyal to God's covenant, and the escalating disasters that will follow if they abandon it.

parts.label: Blessings for loyalty (vv. 1-14)
parts.note: If the people keep God's commands, every part of life will thrive: family, farm, food, travel and battle, with rain arriving on time. Being "the head, not the tail" meant leading and lending rather than following and owing.

parts.label: The blessings turned upside down (vv. 15-35)
parts.note: The curses deliberately mirror the blessings, reversing each one, then pile on disease, drought and defeat. A sky of bronze over ground of iron pictures a drought so long that nothing can fall or grow.

parts.label: Exile and reversal (vv. 36-48)
parts.note: The people and even their king will be carried off to a foreign land, where they end up serving the very idols they were warned against. The root problem named is failing to serve God gladly in good times.

parts.label: Invasion and siege (vv. 49-57)
parts.note: A distant, ruthless army with a foreign language will swoop like an eagle and besiege every city. Starvation becomes so extreme that parents eat their children, a horror the Bible later reports in real sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem.

parts.label: The story run backward (vv. 58-68)
parts.note: A people promised to be as many as the stars will shrink, be scattered, and live in constant dread. Being shipped back to Egypt as unwanted slaves undoes the escape from Egypt that began their story.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this pattern of blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience applies to believers or nations today, or belonged only to ancient Israel's covenant, with many reading it through the New Testament claim that Jesus bore the law's curse.
think: Does the idea that the way a people lives shapes what happens to them ring true to you, and where does it seem to break down?
